faq.q: Can "Quantum Computers" crack AES-256?
faq.a: According to Grover's Algorithm, a quantum computer would effectively halve the security bits of a symmetric cipher. This means AES-128 would be reduced to 64 bits of security (vulnerable), but AES-256 remains at a robust 128 bits of security even against quantum adversaries. This is why 256-bit keys are considered "Quantum-Resistant" for the foreseeable future.

faq.q: Why does my browser lag during encryption?
faq.a: Because this is a local-first tool, your computer's CPU is doing all the heavy lifting. The PBKDF2 process (100,000 hashes) and the AES cipher consume significant computational power to ensure security. This lag is a physical manifestation of the work required to protect your file.

faq.q: What happens if Toolkit Gen goes offline?
faq.a: Since this vault uses standard implementations (Web Crypto API), your files are not "locked" to this specific website. Any tool using AES-256-GCM and PBKDF2-SHA256 can decrypt your file as long as you have the password. Your data security is platform-independent.

faq.q: What is the maximum file size limit for Universal AirDrop?
faq.a: Technically, there is no hard-coded limit because file transfers stream directly between peer devices over WebRTC. However, we recommend a soft limit of 500MB to 1GB per individual file when using mobile devices. Because the transfer protocol temporarily utilizes your web browser's active memory (RAM) as an intermediary buffer, attempting to send an extremely large file (such as a 10GB 4K movie) in a single chunk might cause the browser tab to crash or refresh on older smartphones with limited memory. For massive data transfers, we highly recommend sending multiple smaller files.

faq.q: Does Universal AirDrop use my cellular internet data to send files?
faq.a: No, it does not consume your data plan for the actual file transfer. When using the "Online Connect" mode, the application uses an infinitesimally small amount of internet data (approximately 2 to 5 Kilobytes) to communicate with the signaling server just long enough to generate the 4-digit PIN. Once the "Secure Link Active" badge appears, the internet connection is bypassed entirely. A 5GB file will then transfer directly over your local Wi-Fi router, resulting in 0MB of cellular data usage.

faq.q: Why is my transfer speed slow, or why won't the devices connect?
faq.a: WebRTC connectivity issues usually stem from router configurations. If the devices are stuck on "Connecting...", you may be on a corporate VPN, a strict school network, or a public Wi-Fi access point that enables "Client Isolation" (a security setting that prevents devices on the same Wi-Fi from seeing each other). If the connection establishes but the speed is crawling, ensure both devices are connected to the 5GHz frequency band of your router, rather than the congested 2.4GHz band. If all else fails, use the Offline Hotspot mode, which forces a direct, unhindered connection between the two device's network cards.

faq.q: Are my files saved on Toolkit Gen servers?
faq.a: Absolutely not. Universal AirDrop is designed entirely around a decentralized, serverless architecture. We do not own, operate, or maintain any database capable of storing your media. Your files are never uploaded, cached, or processed by any external cloud storage infrastructure. The transmission happens strictly peer-to-peer (P2P), meaning the data flows directly from the sending device to the receiving device, ensuring maximum privacy and compliance with data protection standards.

faq.a: Mozilla and Apple removed navigator.getBattery() in 2016-2017 because researchers demonstrated that high-resolution battery level readings combined with discharge duration could be used to fingerprint users across private browsing sessions.

faq.q: Can web browsers detect battery cycle count or battery health?

faq.q: What browser workloads cause the fastest laptop battery drain?
faq.a: Unthrottled WebGL/WebGPU graphics loops, software video decoding (when hardware acceleration is disabled), poorly optimized background timer intervals, and excessive CPU main-thread execution consume battery power rapidly.

faq.q: What are the limitations of the Black-Scholes model in modern markets?
faq.a: Black-Scholes assumes constant volatility, constant interest rates, log-normal asset price distributions, and European exercise (no early exercise). Real-world markets exhibit volatility smiles/skews, fat-tailed returns, and American-style early exercise risk.

faq.q: What does Option Theta measure?
faq.a: Theta (\Theta) quantifies the rate of decline in the option's value with the passage of time (time decay), expressed in dollars per share per calendar day. Theta accelerates exponentially in the final 30 days before expiration for at-the-money options.

faq.q: How does dividend yield affect European Call and Put prices?
faq.a: Dividends decrease the future expected price of the underlying stock. A higher continuous dividend yield ($q$) lowers call prices and increases put prices.

faq.q: What is the difference between Delta and probability of expiring ITM?
faq.a: While Delta is often colloquially used as an approximation of the probability that an option will expire in-the-money (ITM), the true risk-neutral probability is $N(d_2)$, whereas Delta is $e^{-qT} N(d_1)$.

faq.q: Can Bluetooth RSSI accurately measure exact distance in meters?
faq.a: No. Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) is inherently noisy and fluctuates due to radio multi-path fading, physical obstructions (walls, bodies, furniture), and antenna polarization. RSSI indicates proximity trends (getting closer vs further) rather than precise metric distances.

faq.q: What RSSI dBm values correspond to proximity ranges?
faq.a: Typically, -30 to -50 dBm indicates immediate proximity (within 1 to 2 feet); -50 to -70 dBm indicates medium proximity (same room, 3 to 10 feet); and -75 to -95 dBm indicates distant proximity or signal blockage through walls.

faq.q: Why does Bluetooth signal fluctuate even when neither device moves?
faq.a: Radio frequency signals in the 2.4GHz ISM band suffer from constructive and destructive interference caused by human movement, domestic Wi-Fi routers, microwave ovens, and physical reflections off metal and mirrors.

faq.q: Why is continuous Bluetooth advertisement tracking restricted on Windows desktop?
faq.a: Windows Bluetooth driver stacks historically limited background advertisement packet monitoring for unpaired web peripherals. Desktop Chrome on macOS and Android provide the most reliable continuous advertisement tracking.

faq.q: What is C2PA and Content Credentials?
faq.a: C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) is an open technical standard developed by Adobe, Microsoft, Intel, and the BBC. It embeds tamper-evident cryptographic manifests into media files, recording who created the file, what software generated or modified it, and whether artificial intelligence was used [Confirmed: C2PA Technical Specifications].

faq.q: How does C2PA detect AI-generated imagery?
faq.a: AI generators that adhere to C2PA standards (such as OpenAI DALL-E 3, Midjourney, and Adobe Firefly) sign an assertion called digitalSourceType set to 'trainedAlgorithmicMedia' or 'compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia'. This assertion is cryptographically sealed into the file manifest.

faq.q: Can C2PA metadata be stripped from an image?
faq.a: Yes. If an image is screenshotted, re-compressed through social media apps (Twitter/X, Facebook) that strip metadata, or converted via basic image converters, the C2PA container is discarded. However, any modification to a C2PA-bearing image without re-signing breaks cryptographic hash validation, immediately flagging the manifest as modified.

faq.q: Does this tool upload my photos to any third-party verification server?
faq.a: No. The entire JUMBF binary box traversal, FourCC scanning, and assertion parsing run locally in your browser memory using an ArrayBuffer parser. Tool inputs are processed locally on your device.

faq.q: When should chest compressions be stopped?

Gamma ($\gamma$) measures side-to-side rotation (Roll). These three signals allow the phone to map any complex 3D rotation with 0.01-degree precision.

faq.q: What is digital dementia?

faq.q: What are healthy screen time limits?

faq.q: What is the difference between sRGB and DCI-P3?
faq.a: DCI-P3 offers approximately 25% more colors than sRGB, particularly in the red and green ranges. sRGB is the web standard used by browsers and operating systems, while DCI-P3 is used for digital cinema projection and increasingly by HDR content creators and gaming monitors.

faq.q: Do I need a wide-gamut monitor for photo editing?
faq.a: For web-delivered photography, a monitor with 95%+ sRGB coverage is sufficient. However, if you work with print output or need to soft-proof Adobe RGB content, a wide-gamut monitor with 90%+ Adobe RGB coverage is essential. Professional photographers often prefer wide-gamut displays with hardware calibration.

faq.q: What does "100% sRGB" actually mean?
faq.a: When a monitor claims "100% sRGB," it means the display can reproduce 100% of the colors within the sRGB color space triangle. However, this doesn't guarantee color accuracy (Delta E). A monitor might cover 100% of sRGB but still produce inaccurate colors. Always check Delta E specifications for true color accuracy.

faq.q: Are QD-OLED monitors worth the premium price?
faq.a: For gaming and HDR video work, QD-OLED monitors offer near-perfect DCI-P3 coverage with infinite contrast ratios and faster response times than LCD panels. The premium is justified if you prioritize visual quality. However, for standard office work or color-accurate photo editing, a professional IPS monitor with hardware calibration may be a better value.

faq.q: What is BT.2020 and do I need it?
faq.a: BT.2020 is the color space defined for Ultra HD HDR content, extending even beyond DCI-P3. While current consumer displays cannot fully reproduce BT.2020 (typically 70-90% coverage), it represents the future of HDR. You don't need it yet, but it's worth considering for future-proofing as more HDR content adopts wider color spaces.

faq.q: How does fatigue affect eye movements?
faq.a: Mental fatigue typically causes increased blink frequency, slower saccadic movements, microsleeps (brief eye closures), and reduced fixation duration. These patterns can signal when your brain needs rest to maintain optimal performance.

faq.q: Why is frame time more informative than average FPS?
faq.a: Average FPS obscures brief, severe pauses. If a game renders 59 frames in 500 milliseconds and spends 500 milliseconds stuck on a single frame, the average frame rate still appears as 60 FPS, even though the user experiences a jarring half-second freeze. Frame time graphs reveal the exact duration of each rendered frame.

faq.q: What do 1% Low and 0.1% Low metrics mean?
faq.a: The 1% Low represents the 99th percentile slowest frame times in a benchmark dataset, converted to an equivalent frame rate. The 0.1% Low captures the single worst 0.1% of stutter frames (the 99.9th percentile). When 1% lows diverge substantially from the average FPS, perceptible stuttering and pacing instability are present.

faq.q: What is the frame budget for a 60 FPS game?
faq.a: At 60 FPS, the GPU and CPU pipeline must render and present each frame in exactly 16.67 milliseconds (1,000ms / 60). At 120 FPS, the budget shrinks to 8.33 milliseconds.

faq.q: What causes uneven frame pacing on consoles or PCs?
faq.a: Uneven frame pacing occurs when frames are rendered at alternating durations (such as 16.6ms followed by 33.3ms), or when the game's internal frame limiter does not align with the display's vertical refresh interval. Proper frame-rate caps or Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) stabilize delivery intervals.

faq.q: Why does 30 FPS look choppy on OLED televisions compared to older LCDs?
faq.a: OLED pixels possess near-instantaneous response times (under 0.1 ms GtG), whereas older LCD panels exhibited 5 to 15 ms of liquid crystal transition blur. On sample-and-hold OLED displays, each 30 FPS frame remains completely static for 33.3 milliseconds before instantly stepping to the next position. Because your retina tracks continuous motion across the screen, this instant stepping creates high-contrast retinal judder. The older LCD panel's slow response time created natural motion blur that masked this stepping [Confirmed: Blur Busters, DisplayMate].

faq.q: Why do 40 FPS console modes require a 120Hz display?
faq.a: On a standard 60Hz display, 40 FPS does not divide evenly: 60 divided by 40 equals 1.5 display refreshes per frame. The television must alternate between holding a frame for 1 refresh (16.67 ms) and 2 refreshes (33.33 ms), creating severe rhythmic 3:2 judder. On a 120Hz display, 120 divided by 40 equals exactly 3.0 refreshes per frame. Every frame is displayed for precisely 25.0 milliseconds in an even 1:1:1 integer cadence, eliminating judder while saving ~33% GPU render budget compared to 60 FPS [Confirmed: Sony Interactive Entertainment, Digital Foundry].

faq.q: What is the HDMI 2.1 VRR 48Hz floor and what is LFC?
faq.a: Standard HDMI 2.1 Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) modules operate within a hardware frequency window of 48 Hz to 120 Hz. When a game's frame rate drops below 48 FPS (such as a 30 FPS title), the display cannot match the frame rate 1:1. The console and display engage Low Framerate Compensation (LFC), which multiplies frames (e.g. duplicating 30 FPS frames twice to refresh at 60 Hz). On OLED televisions, rapid transitions across the 48Hz boundary can cause slight gamma luminance shifts perceived as near-black flicker.

faq.q: Can a web browser diagnose what a PS5 or Xbox outputs directly over HDMI?
faq.a: No. A web browser running on a PC, Mac, or smartphone cannot intercept raw HDMI video signals output from an external console. This diagnostic benchmarks the physical panel's local motion cadence, display refresh synchronization, and browser rendering pipeline to verify your screen's motion reproduction characteristics.

faq.q: Why does my 120Hz or 144Hz screen report 60Hz in this browser test?
faq.a: Common causes include: (1) Operating system display settings defaulted to 60Hz; (2) The connected HDMI or DisplayPort cable does not meet High Speed or Ultra High Speed bandwidth specifications; (3) Browser hardware acceleration is disabled; (4) On Apple Safari for iOS, the 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' feature flag is active by default in Settings.

faq.q: What causes color banding on modern gaming monitors and TVs?
faq.a: Color banding occurs when a display cannot render subtle tonal transitions smoothly. Panels with 8-bit color depth only have 256 shades per RGB channel (16.7 million total colors). When rendering high-dynamic-range content without spatial/temporal dithering (FRC), visible stair-stepping artifacts appear across gradients.

faq.q: What is the 5% gray test and why is it standard for OLEDs?
faq.a: OLED subpixels produce perfect zero-nit blacks when turned off. However, transitioning subpixels from pure black to just above black (1% to 5% luminance) is where manufacturing variations in thin-film transistors (TFTs) become visible, manifesting as subtle vertical stripes or panel vignetting.

faq.q: How does Mini-LED blooming occur?
faq.a: Mini-LED displays use localized full-array backlights divided into hundreds or thousands of physical dimming zones. When a small bright object (such as a star in space or white text) appears against a deep black background, light spills into adjacent pixels within the same dimming zone, creating a noticeable halo or 'blooming' effect.

faq.q: What is 8-bit + FRC versus native 10-bit?
faq.a: A native 10-bit panel has hardware registers to display 1,024 shades per channel (1.07 billion colors). An '8-bit + FRC' (Frame Rate Control) panel uses rapid temporal pixel flickering between two adjacent 8-bit shades to simulate intermediate colors, which can sometimes produce subtle crawling noise in dark gray gradients.

faq.q: How does HRTF simulate 3D audio in ordinary stereo headphones?
faq.a: Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF) model the precise acoustic filtering that occurs as sound waves bounce off your shoulders, head, and ear pinna folds before entering the ear canal. By applying these frequency-dependent filters and microsecond time delays, stereo headphones can convincingly place sounds in 3D space.

faq.q: What is the difference between generic HRTF and personalized SOFA files?
faq.a: Generic HRTF profiles (like the KEMAR acoustic dummy head standardized in the W3C Web Audio PannerNode) use average human measurements. Personalized SOFA (Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics) files contain measured impulse responses tailored to an individual's unique ear anatomy.

faq.q: Why do some spatial audio profiles sound muffled or unnatural?
faq.a: If the simulated HRTF filter curves mismatch your personal pinna geometry, your brain interprets the unexpected notch filters as muffled sound rather than elevated or behind-the-head acoustic cues.

faq.q: What is the formula for calculating model weights VRAM?
faq.a: Model weights memory in gigabytes (GiB) equals (Parameter Count in Billions * Bits per Weight) / (8 * 1.074). For example, an 8.03 billion parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight (Q4_K_M) requires approximately 4.21 GiB of VRAM strictly for weights before loading context buffers.

faq.q: Why does KV cache grow with context length?

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) dramatically reduces this compared to standard multi-head attention.

faq.q: What is the difference between Q4_K_M and Q8_0 quantization?
faq.a: Q8_0 uses 8 bits per weight (~8.5 bits total with scale factors), offering near-lossless output with less than 0.005 perplexity degradation vs FP16. Q4_K_M uses 4-bit medium k-quants (~4.5 bits/weight), reducing memory footprint by nearly 50% while retaining over 98% of benchmark reasoning fidelity.

faq.q: How does Apple Silicon Unified Memory compare to discrete NVIDIA VRAM?
faq.a: Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4 Max and Ultra) shares unified LPDDR5 memory between CPU and GPU cores. While discrete NVIDIA GPUs boast higher memory bandwidth (up to 1,000 GB/s on RTX 4090 vs 400-800 GB/s on Apple Max/Ultra), unified memory allows running 70B and 120B models on 64GB to 128GB unified RAM without expensive multi-GPU PCIe bridges.

faq.q: How does camera rolling shutter detect display flicker?
faq.a: CMOS camera sensors read pixel rows sequentially from top to bottom (rolling shutter). When a display uses PWM to dim its backlight by flashing rapidly on and off, the sensor captures illuminated rows when the backlight is ON and dark bands when the backlight is OFF.

faq.q: Can a smartphone camera measure exact PWM flicker frequency in kHz?
faq.a: No. Smartphone camera rolling shutter frame rates and exposure times are typically limited to between 1/30s and 1/8000s, which can visually reveal flicker up to approximately 480Hz. Precise measurement of high-frequency (e.g. 1920Hz to 3840Hz) flicker requires an optical photodiode connected to an oscilloscope.

faq.q: Why does low-frequency PWM cause headaches and eye strain?
faq.a: Even when screen flicker is too fast to be consciously perceived, the human retina and pupillary sphincter muscles continuously respond to rapid light pulses. This causes micro-contractions in eye muscles, resulting in asthenopia (eye strain), migraines, and visual fatigue.

faq.q: What display technologies eliminate PWM flicker?
faq.a: Displays with DC dimming (analog voltage regulation) or flicker-free LED backlights adjust LED current amplitude rather than pulsing power. High-frequency PWM displays (over 2160Hz) are also significantly more comfortable than low-frequency 240Hz PWM panels.

faq.q: Why does the "Hz Detected" number fluctuate?
faq.a: Modern Operating Systems (Windows/macOS) prioritize hundreds of tasks simultaneously. Browsers use requestAnimationFrame, which attempts to sync with your GPU, but "Jitter" can occur if other apps are consuming CPU resources. For maximum measurement accuracy, close all other browser tabs and background applications like Discord or Steam.

faq.q: Can I use this on my Android phone?
faq.a: Yes. The Software Stroboscope is fully responsive and utilizes the mobile browser's hardware acceleration. In fact, many high-end Android phones now feature 120Hz OLED displays, making them Superior Instruments to standard 60Hz laptops. Open Chrome on your Android, tap the dots, and select "Add to Home Screen" to use it as a standalone tachometer in your workshop.

faq.q: How do I calculate the period of the flash?
faq.a: The period $T$ is the inverse of the frequency. If you are strobing at 10Hz (600 RPM), the period is $1/10 = 0.1$ seconds (100 milliseconds). If your Duty Cycle is 10%, the screen will be white for 10ms and black for 90ms. This high-speed "Pulse-Width" logic is what creates the freezing effect.

faq.q: What is the difference between optical and capacitive tracking?
faq.a: Optical tracking (used in mice) takes thousands of photos of the surface underneath to detect movement. Capacitive tracking (touchpads/phones) detects the electrical conductivity of your skin. Optical is generally more precise for gaming (DPI), while capacitive allows for gestures.

faq.q: What is the difference between input lag and pixel response time?
faq.a: Input lag is the total delay between sending an electrical command (such as pressing a button) and the resulting action appearing on screen. Pixel response time (GtG) is merely the duration required for physical liquid crystal molecules or OLED subpixels to transition between colors. A television can have fast 1ms pixel response time but high 80ms input lag if post-processing is active.

faq.q: How does TV Game Mode reduce input lag?
faq.a: Standard television picture modes route incoming HDMI video through internal digital signal processors (DSPs) to apply noise reduction, motion smoothing (frame interpolation), dynamic contrast, and upscaling. Game Mode bypasses these processing pipelines, cutting input latency from 60ms-120ms down to under 10ms-15ms.

faq.q: What is Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM)?
faq.a: ALLM is an HDMI 2.1 protocol feature that enables a connected console or PC to automatically command the television display to switch into low-latency Game Mode upon launching a game, and revert to normal picture mode when playing a movie.

faq.q: Why does testing at 120Hz feel more responsive than 60Hz?
faq.a: At 60Hz, a new frame is rendered every 16.67 milliseconds. At 120Hz, this interval is cut in half to 8.33 milliseconds. This 8.34ms reduction in scanout latency creates a noticeably tighter connection between user input and onscreen movement.

faq.q: Why is my 120Hz television showing 60Hz in the browser?
faq.a: Several factors can cap browser refresh rates at 60Hz: (1) Windows or macOS display settings may be defaulted to 60Hz; (2) The connected HDMI cable or port may be limited to HDMI 2.0; (3) The television input label may not have 'Enhanced Format' or 'Ultra Deep Color' enabled; (4) The browser hardware acceleration setting may be disabled.

faq.q: What is the difference between HDMI 2.0 and HDMI 2.1?
faq.a: HDMI 2.0 is capped at 18.0 Gbps (TMDS), which permits uncompressed 4K at 60Hz with 8-bit color. HDMI 2.1 expands bandwidth up to 40.0 Gbps (on PS5) and 48.0 Gbps (on Xbox Series X and modern GPUs), enabling uncompressed 4K at 120Hz with 10-bit HDR and Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) simultaneously [Confirmed: HDMI Forum].

faq.q: What is HGiG and why is it recommended over TV Dynamic Tone Mapping?
faq.a: HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group) turns off the television's internal dynamic tone mapping algorithm. This allows the console itself to perform tone mapping directly to the display's exact peak luminance clipping point (e.g., 800 nits on OLED). If both the TV Dynamic Tone Mapping and console HDR are enabled, 'double tone mapping' occurs, blowing out specular highlights.

faq.q: Can a web browser directly detect HDMI cable version?
faq.a: No browser has access to low-level physical EDID pin telemetry due to operating system sandbox protections. Instead, this tool measures the delivered software frame timing and CSS display queries while providing a mathematical bandwidth calculator and verification wizard to validate your configuration.

faq.q: Can a browser sniff USB-C Power Delivery packets without extra hardware?
faq.a: No. Standard computer USB controller chips do not expose raw CC-pin (Configuration Channel) BMC packets to the host operating system. To capture live PD packets, you need an external hardware analyzer (such as a Power-Z or open-source serial sniffer) connected via Web Serial.

faq.q: What is an EPR (Extended Power Range) USB-C contract?
faq.a: USB PD 3.1 Extended Power Range (EPR) increases maximum USB-C power delivery from 100W (20V at 5A) up to 240W (48V at 5A). EPR requires electronically marked 240W cables and specific EPR handshake negotiation.

faq.q: How do USB-C E-marker chips report cable wattage ratings?
faq.a: Electronically marked cables contain a small SOP' responder microchip powered by VCONN on the CC2 line. During initial discovery, the host queries the cable with a Discover Identity command, and the cable replies with maximum supported voltage and current (3A vs 5A).

faq.q: Why are WebGPU TFLOP numbers lower than advertised manufacturer specs?
faq.a: Manufacturer spec sheets quote theoretical peak FP32 throughput assuming 100% compute unit saturation running native Vulkan/DirectX 12 assembly. faq.a: Modern web browsers enforce an explicit security protocol: the Gamepad API remains idle until the user interacts with the controller. Pressing any button (A, Cross, or Trigger) grants permission to stream telemetry.

faq.q: What is an acceptable circularity error score?
faq.a: For factory PlayStation DualSense and Xbox Wireless controllers using potentiometer sensors, circularity errors between 8% and 15% are standard due to mechanical square-gating. High-end Hall Effect controllers (e.g., GuliKit, 8BitDo) typically achieve circularity errors under 2% to 4%.

faq.q: How does potentiometer wear cause stick drift?
faq.a: Potentiometers utilize a physical metal wiper sliding across a resistive carbon film track. Over hundreds of hours, mechanical friction wears away the carbon layer, generating carbon dust and erratic contact resistance that the operating system interprets as phantom stick movement [Confirmed: Hardware teardown analysis].

faq.q: What are Hall Effect sensors and do they eliminate drift?
faq.a: Hall Effect sensors use permanent magnets and non-contact semiconductor sensors to measure magnetic flux density. Because the moving parts never physically touch, they do not suffer from carbon track wear, effectively eliminating physical wear drift for the lifespan of the controller.

faq.q: Can web browsers measure exact Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm?
faq.a: No. The W3C and major browser vendors intentionally do not expose raw Wi-Fi RSSI (received signal strength indicator) or BSSID (access point MAC address) to web applications to prevent geographic location fingerprinting. Browsers only expose estimated connection downlink metrics via navigator.connection.

faq.q: Why does 5 GHz Wi-Fi drop through walls faster than 2.4 GHz?
faq.a: According to electromagnetic propagation physics, higher frequencies attenuate faster when penetrating solid matter. While 5 GHz provides wider channel widths and higher throughput, solid materials like concrete, brick, and tile absorb 5 GHz waves at nearly double the decibel loss of 2.4 GHz waves.

faq.q: How does domestic material attenuation cause dead zones?
faq.a: Drywall and interior wood doors typically cause 2 to 5 dB of signal loss. In contrast, masonry, brick, reinforced concrete, and metal-backed mirrors cause 15 to 30 dB of loss, which can attenuate over 95% of radio frequency energy, producing an immediate dead zone behind the barrier.

faq.q: What is the difference between an extender and a mesh Wi-Fi system?
faq.a: A basic Wi-Fi extender repeats incoming wireless packets on the same frequency band, immediately cutting available throughput by 50% due to half-duplex communication. A mesh system uses dedicated wireless or Ethernet backhaul channels, enabling seamless roaming and full bandwidth across nodes.

faq.q: What is an X.509 certificate?
faq.a: An X.509 certificate is a digital cryptographic document standardized under RFC 5280. It binds an identity (such as a website domain or organization) to a public encryption key using a digital signature from a trusted Certificate Authority [Confirmed: RFC 5280 Specifications].

faq.q: Why are Subject Alternative Names (SANs) preferred over Common Name (CN)?
faq.a: Modern browsers and TLS clients deprecate reliance on the Subject Common Name (CN) field due to ambiguity and lack of multi-domain support. RFC 6125 mandates that hostname validation rely exclusively on the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension [Confirmed: RFC 6125].

faq.q: Are my private keys exposed if I decode a certificate here?
faq.a: No. An X.509 public certificate contains only the public key and identity metadata; it never contains the private key. Furthermore, this tool processes all parsing locally in browser RAM without server transmission.

faq.q: How does the tool calculate the certificate fingerprint?
faq.a: The fingerprint is computed by running the SHA-256 or SHA-1 cryptographic hash algorithm over the entire raw binary DER encoding of the certificate using the browser Native Web Cryptography API.

faq.q: Why is usable ZFS capacity less than raw drive manufacturer size?
faq.a: Drive manufacturers market drives using decimal terabytes (1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes), whereas ZFS and operating systems allocate space in binary tebibytes (1 TiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes). Additionally, ZFS reserves ~3% slop space for internal metadata and copy-on-write overhead.

faq.q: Why is the 80% pool capacity rule important in ZFS?
faq.a: ZFS uses a copy-on-write transaction model. When a pool exceeds 80% capacity, the space allocator switches from first-fit to best-fit algorithms, resulting in severe write performance degradation and fragmentation.

faq.q: What is the minimum recommended drive count for RAIDZ2?
faq.a: While RAIDZ2 can function with 4 drives, 6 to 8 drives per vdev is standard engineering practice to balance parity overhead (33% to 25%) with high fault tolerance.

faq.q: When should I deploy a SLOG or L2ARC cache device?
faq.a: A dedicated SLOG (Separate ZFS Intent Log) device on high-write endurance NVMe is recommended for synchronous write workloads (NFS, databases, VM storage). L2ARC is recommended when your active working dataset exceeds physical RAM.
